title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab

evidence_basis.summary_text: Felipe Blanes, identified in the recording metadata and introducing himself as a member of Amazon AGI Lab, describes lessons from customer enablement for Nova Act browser agents. evidence_basis.summary_text: In this workshop opening, Priyanka, identified in recording metadata as Priyanka Phatak, introduces Claude Managed Agents alongside Gabe Cemaj. She describes agents as models calling tools in a loop, supported by a harness and an isolated execution environment. Harnesses encode model-specific assumptions: context resets addressed Sonnet 4.5's premature task completion near its context limit but were unnecessary for Opus 4.5. Anthropic initially placed the session log, harness, and sandbox in one container, creating fragile state, ambiguous failures, restricted debugging around customer data, and awkward customer-network integration. The redesign separates a durable append-only session log, a replaceable brain comprising Claude and its harness, and independently provisioned hands comprising sandboxes and tools. A replacement harness can resume from the log, while sandbox failures become tool errors Claude can respond to. Credentials are injected through an external proxy rather than exposed inside the sandbox. Persisting the full event history also permits different context-compaction strategies without rewriting the history. Priyanka reports about 90% lower time to first token from starting inference before provisioning a sandbox; the accompanying engineering article separately specifies roughly 60% lower p50 and over 90% lower p95. The workshop then outlines a joke-teller agent: configure an environment, define the agent's model, prompt, and tools, create a session, and exchange events, including custom-tool requests and results. This recording ends as the console quick start begins.
summary_key_points: Harness workarounds depend on model behavior. Separating interfaces lets the harness change when those assumptions become stale.
The session log preserves continuity while the harness and sandbox remain replaceable. Sandbox failure returns a decision to Claude; harness failure is recovered by reading the log.
Injecting tokens at an outbound proxy keeps credentials out of the sandbox and away from model-visible requests to print or save them.
Preserved events support different context strategies, while on-demand sandbox provisioning lets inference begin sooner. Anthropic reports about 90% lower time to first token.
An environment and agent definition create an idle session; events start its work, carry custom tool exchanges, report state and allow interruption.

title: Why AI Didn't Actually Make You Ship Faster — Gabriel Spencer-Harper, Meticulous

evidence_basis.summary_text: Gabriel Spencer-Harper, introduced in the supplied recording context as Meticulous’s co-founder and CEO, argues that AI code generation shifts the delivery bottleneck to review and verification. He says handwritten assertions cannot exhaustively anticipate regressions across feature flags, roles, permissions and configurations. Near-exhaustive verification, minimal developer effort, customer deployment breadth and comparative flakiness are presented as the speaker’s claims, without independent performance validation in the supplied recording.
summary_key_points: Faster code generation can leave verification as the limiting step: the team still needs to understand a change across roles, permissions, flags and configurations.
Meticulous compares recorded workflows before and after a change. It exposes visible differences; a person or agent decides whether they are expected.
Recorded network responses make replay repeatable and isolate tests for parallel execution. Browser-level timing control addresses variation that network mocking cannot remove.

Coverage-guided selection depends on frequent screenshots to turn executed paths into visually checked paths. At large screenshot volumes, controlling flakiness is essential to keeping the differences useful.

title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
reason: Evaluation workshop with human-verdict holdouts, judge bias/calibration, disagreement analysis, policy context and CI gates.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Tejas Kumar presents a hands-on workshop on evaluating nondeterministic AI systems, describing evals as predeployment reliability instrumentation that complements runtime agent harnesses. He outlines test cases, expected behavior, judges and aggregation, then discusses deterministic checks, schema validation, pairwise and pointwise judgments. He warns that position bias, sycophancy, self-preference and verbosity can distort LLM judgments.

Using TypeScript and Vitest, Kumar shows a return-policy answer incorrectly passing a substring test merely because it contains “cannot.” He replaces the matcher with an LLM judge, observes a preference for a model-generated answer, and improves the result by supplying a fourteen-day return policy. He then evaluates approximately thirty scenarios against withheld human verdicts, normalizes response casing, investigates disagreements, adds missing policy details and switches from GPT-3.5 Turbo to GPT-4o mini. A loyal-customer example prompts an explicit rule that the policy cannot be waived. One run yields twenty-seven agreements out of thirty; a subsequent aggregate test passes at his chosen 80% agreement threshold.

Kumar recommends version-pinned judges and continuously refreshed, human-reviewed production examples. An OpenRAG demonstration initially finds no supporting sources, then retrieves a newly uploaded refund policy and denies a twenty-day return. Docling processes the document and OpenSearch stores the indexed knowledge. He recommends starting with inexpensive deterministic checks and trace validation before using model judges. Audience questions cover synthetic adversarial examples, responsibility for evaluating coding-agent skills, and sharing a living policy source between the production agent and judge. His numerical thresholds and broad claims about bias, security incidents and perfect agreement remain attributed workshop guidance rather than independently established guarantees.
summary_key_points: Evals exercise behavior before deployment; harness controls protect execution at runtime. Both are needed when agents read untrusted content or use consequential tools.
A substring assertion can pass the wrong decision. The headphone example turns green because “cannot” describes shipping rather than return eligibility.
Calibrate a judge against human verdicts it cannot see. Normalize formatting differences, inspect substantive disagreements, add missing policy, and change models when context is insufficient.
The workshop’s CI gate measures aggregate human–judge agreement at an 80% threshold. Passing that gate establishes agreement on the collected cases, not complete production coverage.
Keep policy shared and cases current: retrieve the same rules for the agent and judge, add human-labeled production examples, and use synthetic adversarial cases to explore likely failures.

title: Stop Chunking Like It's 2022 — Yuval Belfer, AI21 Labs
reason: Retrieval experiments compare six chunk sizes, an oracle baseline and multi-scale RRF across named datasets with memory/latency tradeoffs.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Yuval Belfer argues that effective chunk size depends on the query, making a single indexing-time choice a source of retrieval loss. Small chunks preserve focused details but lose broader context; large chunks retain context while diluting specific information. Experiments indexing datasets at six sizes, contrasting Seinfeld questions, and an answer-informed oracle illustrate this tradeoff. Belfer reports an oracle gap of roughly 20–40 percent, without specifying whether that means relative improvement or percentage points. His practical approach indexes multiple window sizes, queries every index, maps retrieved chunks to whole documents, and combines document rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. He reports matching or beating the best fixed-size approach across QMSum, NarrativeQA, Seinfeld, and FinanceBench. The stated tradeoff is roughly two to five times the memory, with little added latency from parallel retrieval and inexpensive fusion. Selecting the number and sizes of windows and improving fusion remain open research questions.
summary_key_points: The useful chunk size depends on the question: narrow windows can find contained facts while losing relationships that need surrounding context.
The oracle's reported 20%–40% recall gap measures headroom using known answers. It cannot choose a scale for an unanswered query.
Multiscale indexing searches N window sizes, maps chunk matches to whole documents, and combines comparable document rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

Belfer reports matching or beating the best fixed size across four datasets at roughly two to five times the memory. Parallel searches limit added latency; scale selection and better fusion remain open questions.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Kent C. Dodds develops product engineering judgment through two interactive exercises. A request for facial recognition in a workshop check-in app becomes a Jobs to Be Done statement: help attendees enter quickly so they can learn without missing the first 20 minutes. He argues that asking why, examining the problem tree, and considering functional, social, and emotional needs exposes alternatives such as parallel queues or NFC badges while revealing the discomfort facial data collection may cause. Feedback aggregation and repeated product use help assess whether users actually make progress. Audience questions address validating problems through The Mom Test and prototypes, checking whether one demanding customer's needs generalize, and understanding architecture when guiding agents during consequential incidents. A food delivery exercise introduces the Kano model: reliable confirmations are basic needs, delivery estimate accuracy is a performance need, and discounts or shared carts can delight. GPS tracking illustrates changing expectations. Dodds maps these categories to reliable foundations, measured quality, and reversible experiments; indifferent features add maintenance costs, while unwanted features warrant pushback. He closes by arguing that technical expertise combined with understanding user problems remains valuable as AI accelerates implementation.

Validate problems through past behavior and observed prototype use; a customer’s proposed solution may not represent other customers’ needs.

title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
reason: End-to-end model evaluation fixes tasks, sources and acceptance criteria, measuring trustworthy results, retries, human repair, cost and repeatability.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Morgan Suo presents M3.1 Flash through a practical question: whether a model that generates faster actually shortens the time and lowers the cost required to produce a usable result. The example is an analyst researching whether printed-circuit-board suppliers are converting AI-server demand into cash. A satisfactory report must use the correct company reports and reporting periods, keep businesses separate, expose sources behind important claims, support recalculation, and identify evidence that could change the conclusion. The distinction between rising profit and cash generation illustrates why source disclosures and cash-flow statements matter.

The talk connects that workflow to several M3.1 Flash optimizations. Sparse attention reduces work over long inputs but must still retrieve decisive passages such as short footnotes. In one separate long-context test, the model reportedly passed 39 requests with inputs reaching about 830,000 tokens, though the speaker calls for additional tests on real reports. The model changes KV-cache keys and values from 8 bits to 4 bits while retaining 8-bit queries, and selected mixture-of-experts components use 4-bit weights and activations. These changes can reduce storage, data movement, or computation, but aggregate benchmark averages can conceal regressions that matter to a particular user.

Speculative decoding can obtain several accepted tokens from one target-model check, yet drafting, verification, rejection, retrieval, tool calls, and retries all contribute to elapsed time. A separate serving test increased concurrency from 32 to 64 and raised total output by about 1.9× while substantially worsening P95 time to first token; the exact upper latency value is unclear in the ASR. Reasoning controls create another trade-off: in the cited coding test, high reasoning used fewer output tokens than maximum reasoning, while accuracy was reported as falling from 80% to 68%.

The recommended model-switch evaluation fixes the question, source reports, information cutoff, and acceptance criteria in advance. It then measures report trustworthiness, the full cost and time of producing an acceptable report—including failed attempts and human repair—and repeatability under recorded model versions, runtime versions, prompts, settings, and sources. The operational advice is to test at expected load, preserve failure examples, begin with a limited rollout, and retain a rollback path. The central criterion is the time and cost required to deliver a correct, checkable report when needed, rather than isolated token speed or throughput.
summary_key_points: Measure time and cost to an acceptable report, including retrieval, retries, failed attempts and human repair.
Sparse attention reduces work by selecting text blocks, so test whether important evidence remains findable at different positions in real documents.
Lower precision can reduce data movement, but near-identical average scores can conceal changes on individual tasks; full-setup comparisons do not isolate their causes.
Test serving load and reasoning effort against the deadline and quality needed for the actual job, rather than relying on throughput or first-token latency alone.

title: The 6 Pillars of an Agentic Harness for Production — Varun Krovvidi, Resolve AI
reason: Production harness includes multi-level evaluations of investigation paths, engineer comparisons and confidence calibration, rather than only final answers.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Varun Krovvidi, introduced as part of Resolve AI, describes a six-pillar agentic harness for running and fixing production software. He contrasts self-documenting, modular, single-domain code with production work spanning infrastructure, telemetry, code, and multiple teams; he estimates that running and fixing software consumes 70% of engineering time. He identifies five scaling problems: anchoring bias and changing model capabilities, excessive or insufficient context, coherent answers without causal evidence, inadequate guardrails, and missing learning across investigations. His proposed pillars are model orchestration, context engineering, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning systems, and evals. These involve continuously evaluating task-specific model choices, supplying precise context and tool queries, grounding root causes in causal evidence with lower confidence when evidence is incomplete, restricting read/write actions, retaining investigation and user feedback, and evaluating reinforcement, investigation paths, engineer comparisons, and confidence calibration. In the demo, Resolve AI picks up a Grafana alert in Slack and investigates across code, infrastructure, knowledge bases, and observability. Krovvidi reports stale integrations as the root cause, shows competing explanations including a coincident GCP outage, and demonstrates evidence-based pushback when challenged and teammate collaboration through Slack. He closes by distinguishing this reasoning architecture from the robust platform also needed to productize AI.
summary_key_points: Production investigations combine code, infrastructure, knowledge and telemetry across teams; a capable model needs a harness that manages those connections.

Model orchestration must both reassess new models and route individual tasks. Context engineering must supply enough information to explore useful paths, then narrow retrieval through precise tool calls.
A root-cause claim requires a causal chain of evidence. When the chain cannot be established, the system should lower confidence and indicate another investigative direction.
Permissions determine which proposed fixes can become actions; learning and evals determine whether later investigations improve, including their reasoning paths and confidence.
The demo’s central test is whether a diagnosis remains grounded when an engineer suggests coincident outages or deployment errors, while preserving a shared investigation for teammates.

title: Harness Engineering: How to Build a Software Factory — Dru Knox, Tessl
reason: Harness engineering separates cheap inner checks, independent outer verification/mutation testing and meta feedback loops with stable quality targets.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Dru Knox, who introduces himself as Tessl's head of product and design at presentation time, describes harness engineering as building the loops that automate and improve a software factory. In his definition, agents create the shipped product while engineers build the system that produces it. He distinguishes autonomy—less human correction—from automation—less manual review and verification—and argues that teams should improve both while maintaining quality, ultimately using additional capacity for better tests, refactors and exploration. His framework has cheap, frequent inner-loop checks before a PR; more expensive outer-loop verification after a PR, such as agentic QA and mutation testing; and a meta loop that learns from logs, PRs, issues and user feedback to prevent repeated mistakes. He identifies rapidly changing practices, unplanned improvement work and inaccessible workflow signals as obstacles. The proposed foundation comprises a legible control plane, agent-ready infrastructure and ongoing improvement loops. Knox then presents Tessl's governed skills registry, Linear-to-GitHub connectors, code-review tools, Tessl Agent for discovering and automating recurring work, and Tessl Launch for running skills with selected coding agents in permissioned sandboxes. He recommends tracking fewer manual takeovers and human PR comments, more PRs initiated without human input, and stable then improving product quality. The product capabilities and anticipated benefits are the speaker's claims, rather than independently measured outcomes.
summary_key_points: Autonomy measures how much correction an agent needs; automation measures how much work can proceed without manual verification. Improve both while tracking product quality.
Run cheap checks during development, expensive checks on PRs, and a meta loop across logs, reviews and user feedback to improve future attempts.
Shared issues, sandboxed agent runs and PR comments make human corrections available for later analysis; reusable skills distribute what the team learns.
A recurring task such as a flaky-test hunt can become a skill and an automated workflow, reducing the separate effort required to start each run.

title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
reason: Judge refers to GraphSAGE/XGBoost fraud classification, not an LLM judge; conventional classifier metrics do not make this an agent-evaluation talk.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Somya Rai and MD Sharique, identified in the recording metadata with EXL, describe adding GraphSAGE embeddings to an existing XGBoost fraud classifier. Their objective is better detection within a fixed analyst alert budget. They report true positive rates rising from 36% to 48% for card-present transactions and from 48% to 61% for online transactions, approximately 33% and 27% relative improvements at matched alert rates. These are speaker-reported results, not an independently validated benchmark. Sampling preserves selected users’ transaction histories and fraud users’ genuine transactions as hard negatives. Disjoint monthly graphs, earlier-timestamp neighbors, excluded fraud labels and training-only preprocessing address leakage. The architecture combines mean, maximum and standard deviation aggregation with entity-history and temporal features; the speakers favor 128-dimensional embeddings. Subgraph attribution supplies linked-transaction evidence for analyst review. Serving uses offline cached representations and a small online forward pass with an XGBoost head. The speakers describe moving from transaction-node caches to user and merchant embeddings, reducing the stated footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2–3 GB, and report 2.3 ms median and 3.1 ms P99 latency. The approximately $65 million headline is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, not demonstrated realized savings; its relationship to the portfolio dollar figures is unresolved.
summary_key_points: Graph embeddings add neighborhood information to XGBoost. The reported 27–33% relative detection gains compare the combined system with a tuned tabular baseline at matched alert rates.
Sampling must preserve useful connectivity: retain selected users’ histories, keep legitimate transactions from fraud-associated users as hard negatives, and balance training batches downstream.
Monthly graph separation, earlier-timestamp aggregation, target exclusion and training-only preprocessing address different leakage routes.
Mean, maximum and standard deviation preserve different neighborhood signals; maximum pooling keeps a single suspicious neighbor from disappearing into an average.

Caching removes graph-sized work from each request, but memory and freshness remain constraints. User-and-merchant embeddings reduce the stated cache from 60 GB to 2–3 GB; the final reported latency is 3.1 milliseconds at P99.

title: The Best Models Still Reason Like Toddlers — Andrew Dai, Elorian
reason: Examines whether visual benchmarks expose counting, spatial grounding and video state-tracking failures rather than pattern recognition.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Andrew Dai argues that frontier models often substitute pattern recognition for detailed visual reasoning, leading to counting, spatial grounding, and video state-tracking errors. He questions whether common benchmarks capture these weaknesses and describes an approach combining specialized data, synthetic training, architectural changes, and visual chain of thought. He presents robotics, construction safety, and mechanical design as potential applications.
summary_key_points: Dai uses a partial chessboard and Catan road counting to illustrate models answering from familiar patterns rather than inspecting the visible scene.

He describes models missing robot actions and losing track of state across long videos. His practical distinction between understanding and reasoning is whether a person needs more than a second to inspect the scene.
He criticizes low-resolution reasoning tasks and multimodal questions answerable without inspecting their images, calling for benchmarks that test geometry and spatial intelligence.
The proposed approach combines visual reasoning data, a synthetic data flywheel using evaluations, agents, SFT and RL, transformer architecture improvements, and visual chain of thought.
His visual chain-of-thought example identifies hotels with bounding boxes before narrowing to the red hotels, making intermediate reasoning steps visual.

He proposes action-relevant scene understanding for robots, connecting construction video to written safety policies, and extracting geometric logic for design with programmatic or simulation validation.

title: How Secrets Leak Through AI Agents (and How to Stop It) — Venice AI
reason: Primary content: Joshua Mo, who introduces himself as Venice AI's lead developer relations engineer at the time of the talk and a former Rig lead maintainer, argues that privacy depends on the entire agent system. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Joshua Mo, who introduces himself as Venice AI's lead developer relations engineer at the time of the talk and a former Rig lead maintainer, argues that privacy depends on the entire agent system. He describes Venice's approach as avoiding stored prompts and conversations, anonymizing requests to external providers, using trusted execution environments, and encrypting stored results with split-key custody. He identifies logs and credentials passed into the LLM reasoning layer as exposure paths, including possible exfiltration through tool calls. His proposed patterns include hashed identifiers, revocable access handles, narrow tool scope, prompt-injection screening, and connecting credential vaults to the execution layer so the model does not receive secrets. He warns that sandboxes still permit data leakage through network access and recommends permission monitoring and control over the runtime. He closes with attested confidential inference and the unresolved challenge of combining encrypted tool calls with ergonomic APIs. Privacy guarantees, encryption descriptions, training-data risks, and context-performance benefits are presented as speaker claims.
summary_key_points: Reducing retained sensitive data reduces what a breach can expose; application logs can recreate exposure even when the model provider retains no conversations.
Connect the credential vault to execution so the model can request an action without receiving the secret needed to perform it.
Narrow tool scope and prompt-injection screening address different risks. Internet-enabled sandboxes still require permission monitoring.
Attested confidential inference protects the reasoning environment; ergonomic, fully encrypted tool calls remain an unresolved part of the design presented here.

title: Your LLM Judge Is a Confident Liar: Building Better Verifiers — Browserbase
reason: Universal Verifier: task-specific rubrics, screenshot evidence, process/outcome scores, human agreement and held-out verifier labels.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Miguel González Fernández and Corby Rosset present the Universal Verifier for evaluating computer-use and web-agent trajectories. They explain why changing websites, environmental blockers and multiple valid paths made deterministic evaluations difficult to maintain, while unreliable LLM judges could corrupt both benchmark scores and training signals. For Fara-7B on WebVoyager, they report approximately 74% success under the benchmark's GPT-4o judge versus 38% under their verifier. Their approach generates task-specific rubrics, ranks screenshots for relevance to each criterion, checks agent claims against visual evidence, and produces separate process and binary outcome scores. Rubrics should grade only requested work and isolate errors; an environmental blocker can permit full process credit while leaving the user's goal unmet. Human-label validation yielded outcome Cohen's kappa of about 0.58 on the Browserbase dataset, comparable to human inter-annotator agreement. The talk describes false positives falling from nearly half to zero; the supplied paper more precisely reports outcome false-positive rates of 1% internally and 8% on the Browserbase dataset. The presenters also report better supervised fine-tuning results when training on verifier-filtered trajectories at fixed dataset sizes. An autoresearch loop completed roughly three weeks of experimentation in one day but reached about 70% of expert agreement when starting without expert prompts; continuing expert work improved results further. They release code and CUAVerifierBench labels through microsoft/fara. Q&A covers planned desktop verification using logs and telemetry, and holding out roughly two-thirds of labels to limit overfitting.
summary_key_points: Generate task-specific criteria, retrieve relevant screenshot evidence for each one, and compare the agent’s claims with the visible environment.
Keep process credit separate from task completion: an accurate attempt blocked by unavailable inventory can deserve full process marks while still failing the purchase goal.
Penalize an upstream mistake where it occurs, preserving credit for correctly performed downstream work without declaring the overall answer correct.
Evaluate a verifier through held-out human judgments and the quality of models trained on its selected data.

The Opus 4.6 autoresearch run completed roughly thirty experiments in a day but reached about 70% of the human-built verifier’s agreement; a run primed with human findings exceeded the team’s previous result.

He compares five approaches to crossing information silos under privacy constraints, favors AI-maintained shared knowledge for near-term benefits, and discusses automated disclosure policies, failure modes, and potential collaboration across companies.
summary_key_points: He proposes evaluating multi-agent systems by how closely they approximate an agent with access to all relevant information, while treating privacy and security as constraints on that access.
Shared trust boundaries simplify access, but he argues that they preserve silos and continue to require human coordination as models improve.
Custom tools can expose limited outputs, such as relationship-strength scores derived from email, but require humans to design and explain the privacy trade-offs.

Human-mediated requests can burden many people. His black-box alternative searches private information first and seeks approval only from owners of information needed for the result or action, requiring trust in its access and disclosure controls.
He warns about prompt injection, persistent errors in shared knowledge, unintended disclosures, and unresolved questions about approvals, logging, reversibility, and auditing.

He recommends starting automated sharing with low-sensitivity information and retaining human review for other disclosures. He sees cross-company information sharing as an opportunity, while expressing uncertainty about trusting agents with privacy decisions.

title: Inside 847 Production Clinical AI Notes — Sebastian Fox, Composo
reason: Clinical-note error analysis and context-dependent grading use expert corrections, retrieved examples and continuous discovery of harmful changes.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Sebastian Fox examines harmful additions, changes, and omissions in AI-generated clinical notes and argues that static evaluation rubrics struggle to judge which differences matter. He proposes continuously discovering failures from real outputs, capturing expert reasoning and corrections, and retrieving relevant examples and references for each evaluation. He reports better performance from this approach on the dataset presented.
summary_key_points: Apparently plausible notes can conceal consequential omissions or misrepresent a consultation's final decision, even when their wording comes from the transcript.
Fox cites a real-world study reporting potentially seriously harmful errors in about one in 20 notes, important omissions in nearly one in five, and hallucinations in more than one in 10.

In his evaluation of notes generated by three production ambient scribes, a checker using a detailed rubric and supporting checks still passed notes containing serious errors; he reports such errors in one fifth of its clean passes.
He distinguishes detecting differences from judging their importance: expert judgment is tacit, contextual, and changing, so a fixed rubric cannot fully capture it.
His proposed loop discovers failure modes in real outputs, captures expert reasoning and corrections, and assembles relevant prior judgments, references, and guidelines for each new note.

Fox reports that the example-calibrated judge outperformed two rubric-based approaches on the same notes. He recommends starting with experts leaving free-form comments on real outputs and continuing evaluation as standards evolve.

title: Same GPU, 50% More Output: Why the Operator Matters — Oliver Kennon, SemiAnalysis

Useful output must also satisfy quality, latency, availability, and security requirements. Kennon says ClusterMAX assesses managed GPU clusters using provisioning, reliability, monitoring, security, documentation, hands-on testing, customer feedback, pricing, and availability, while cautioning that managed-cluster ratings do not automatically apply to bare-metal offerings. He distinguishes GPU rental prices from an inference producer's total production cost and recommends dividing all delivery spending by usable output. Cost-curve position is relative: a producer may improve yet fall behind faster-improving competitors, while temporary scarcity can conceal cost disadvantages. summary_key_points: GPU-hours measure an input. The better economic metric is full cost per successfully completed task at the required quality; comparable price per token is only a practical proxy.

Useful intelligence requires quality, latency, availability, and security. Fast GPUs do not rescue a service that exposes another customer’s logs or cannot sustain production operation.

Rental price, production cost, and selling price are separate numbers. Operations create an advantage only when their added cost is justified by more acceptable output and the process remains effective as workloads change.

Compute grades and operator ratings can support credible rental benchmarks and futures, but a rental-price hedge cannot repair deployment failures or cover every component of inference production cost.

title: Your Fridge Is a Valid Payment Device — Eleonora Drykina & Nina Žižakić, In The Pocket

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Nina Žižakić and Eleonora Drykina, who introduce themselves as working at In The Pocket at the time of the talk, describe a rulebook RAG assistant for an anonymous Belgian payments client. Its corpus contains about 270 PDFs, 6,000 pages and 3,000 tables, with frequent references between documents. Answers must cite the rulebook, section and page while excluding unsupported payment-scheme details from the model's general knowledge.

The indexing pipeline packs paragraphs into roughly 2,000-character, non-overlapping chunks without splitting tables. Section paths and chunk indices support citations and reconstruction of larger passages. Tables become CSV with repeated fields to preserve relationships otherwise lost during plain-text extraction. Retrieval combines dense search and BM25 in Qdrant using reciprocal rank fusion: 50 results from each become 30 fused candidates, reranked for section coherence before sending 10 to the agent. On 63 retrieval-only evaluation questions, the speakers report a hit-rate increase from 92% to 97%; this is not an end-to-end answer-accuracy result.

Four tools let the agent search, retrieve sections, retrieve small full rulebooks and list available rulebooks. Documents above roughly 100,000 tokens return a section list instead of their full contents, and a prompt asks the agent to reconsider redundant searches before a sixth call. Median answer latency is 38 seconds. The interface streams Markdown immediately and appends a completed source card, replacing an earlier structured-output design that delayed all visible content.

Azure Table Storage records questions, tool calls, answers, feedback and interaction events; conversation context is limited to 20 messages. About 86 end-to-end Promptfoo tests combine rubric-based judging with citation checks, alongside the separate retrieval evaluation. The speakers caution that judge changes need reruns: five of 12 result flips did not reproduce, and one allegedly hallucinated date was actually in the source. The internal rollout had reached 34 users and roughly 900 questions across more than 100 conversations; external release remained planned. Their closing lessons emphasize document structure, table processing, multiple retrieval scales, streaming and early user testing.
summary_key_points: Non-overlapping chunks, section paths and chunk indexes let the agent reconstruct larger passages instead of relying only on isolated search hits.
Repeating merged table labels in CSV preserves which categories apply to each row, reducing the risk of retrieving a fee under the wrong heading.
Hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval raised the reported retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions; this was not an end-to-end answer accuracy result.
Broader retrieval needs bounded tools: oversized documents return section lists, invalid section names return valid alternatives, and repeated searches trigger reconsideration.
Streaming Markdown separately from a completed source card made a median 38-second answer progressively readable.
Evaluation changes need investigation: judge decisions can vary between runs, and an incorrect rubric can penalize a fact that is present in the source.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Simran Arora explains how communication between GPUs constrains AI workloads and presents ParallelKittens primitives for writing efficient multi-GPU kernels. Efficient kernels require choosing among copy-engine, TMA, and register-level transfers, and deciding how to overlap computation and communication within or across streaming multiprocessors. These choices involve message size, resource use, data alignment, and support for in-network reductions.
ParallelKittens packages these ideas into primitives and templates, typically adding roughly a dozen lines to a single-GPU kernel. Arora reports production use at Together AI and Cursor.

ParallelKernelBench contains 87 problems drawn from repositories and existing implementations. Tasks supply an unoptimized PyTorch reference and hardware topology, asking models to generate efficient CUDA kernels using unified virtual addressing.

The best tested model solved 28 of 87 problems zero-shot, with 22 faster than the baseline. Multiple samples increased correctness to 36 problems, while the share both correct and faster plateaued near 31%.

Arora attributes persistent failures to reasoning about collective ordering, data partitioning, scheduling, and transfer selection. A multi-turn agent with bash access increased solved problems from 24 to 35, with 26 beating the reference, but further time also produced a plateau.

title: Homa: The End of TCP for AI Clusters — John Ousterhout, Stanford

evidence_basis.summary_text: John Ousterhout argues that AI inference and agentic workloads increasingly depend on small coordination exchanges, making tail latency important alongside bulk throughput. A single slow synchronization exchange can stall distributed computation and leave GPUs idle. He attributes delays to incast queues, lagging sender-driven congestion control, and byte-stream head-of-line blocking. He presents Homa, a Stanford-developed transport using independent RPC messages, shortest remaining processing time, receiver-issued packet grants, and switch priority queues to favor short messages. In the sample mixed-message benchmark he describes, Homa delivers roughly 13× lower short-message P99 latency than TCP and nearly 2× better latency for the longest messages. These are reported benchmark results, rather than demonstrated end-to-end AI application speedups. At the time of the talk, he says a Linux kernel module is available on GitHub and upstreaming is in progress, and invites developers to experiment with Homa.
summary_key_points: A barrier makes the slowest required exchange determine when GPU computation resumes. Short-message tail latency matters increasingly when compute phases themselves take milliseconds.
Incast builds a queue at the receiver’s last hop. Sender-side congestion feedback must travel back before several senders can adjust, while competing transfers continue to change.

Homa keeps message lengths visible and messages independent. Receiver grants pace scheduled traffic and favor messages with less work remaining; switch priorities let short messages pass queued bulk packets.

The presented benchmark reports about thirteenfold better short-message P99 latency and almost twofold better performance for the longest messages versus TCP. Application throughput gains and comparisons with RoCE require separate measurements.

title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore

evidence_basis.summary_text: Corey Gallon presents three cumulative levels of agent review for overstated completion, factual errors and faulty reasoning. Level one requires a verified artifact and fingerprint, or an explicit missing-artifact report, followed by the dispatching agent's own check. evidence_basis.summary_text: Al Chen describes deploying production AI observability systems in highly regulated banks, where proving how a result was obtained matters as much as the result itself. Rather than treating a package-version bump as proof, his proposed workflow uses an agent harness to reproduce an older exploit against the updated application and generate tests showing whether the vulnerability remains. Second, disaster recovery for ClickHouse requires more than successful backup and restore logs: teams should compare row counts and verify replica convergence to establish current data correctness. Cross-region replication also creates data-residency decisions, so one pattern is to replicate IDs and metadata while keeping core trace data within its required jurisdiction. Third, redaction in the user interface does not guarantee privacy because an LLM judge's persisted reasoning can reproduce PII or MNPI from raw traces. Mitigations include retaining scores while conditionally suppressing reasoning, or running a second judge over redacted input when reviewers need an explanation. Chen argues that zero leakage and data sovereignty carry real compute and engineering costs. Deployment timelines depend on evidence, security reviews, image-ingestion processes, available GPUs, LLM gateways, RBAC, and organizational approval paths; many delays arise from human coordination rather than purely technical work. The central recommendation is to increase compliance velocity by showing the work and converting customer concerns into explicit engineering, workflow, and organizational workstreams.

title: Why Humans Can't Keep Up With AI-Written Code - Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
reason: Factory quality methodology examines unreliable LLM judgments, success-rate-dependent task horizons, independent verification and auditable evidence.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Tariq Shaukat, who introduces himself as Sonar's CEO, argues that enterprise agentic software factories should optimize for confidence in shipped software rather than code volume. He uses Toyota and Lexus manufacturing practices to frame quality as a property engineered into the production system: prioritize quality, fix systemic causes, design components to fit together, resolve problems early and empower people to stop the line. He connects these principles to established software practices before describing how agents disrupt the production process.

He identifies five challenges: human review that cannot scale and is vulnerable to cognitive surrender; agents struggling to navigate large, complex codebases; errors compounding across long tasks; inconsistent LLM judgments; and shrinking time to exploit vulnerabilities. To illustrate the gap between production and delivery, he cites a study reporting increases of 2,450% in lines of code and 240% in commits, but only 30% in releases. He also cautions that task-completion horizons depend on the required success rate and that repeated or challenged LLM judgments can change.

Sonar's proposed code confidence formula multiplies four elements: clear intent, guide rails that steer agents, independent and thorough verification, and consistent, auditable, repeatable evidence. Shaukat treats each element as necessary: a missing factor undermines confidence in the whole factory. He describes Sonar Vortex as supplying intent, guidance and in-loop verification, reporting 36% lower token cost and 92% fewer issues in commits. He presents SonarQube verification as combining deterministic and agentic methods. In a customer survey comparison, he reports that SonarQube users were more likely than non-users to perceive very positive AI-coding impacts on security, time to market and outage frequency; these are reported perceptions, not measured percentage reductions in incidents or delivery time. He closes by emphasizing quality gates, compliance evidence and the distinction between abundant code and scarce confidence.
summary_key_points: Code generation and software delivery are different measures. The study presented reports increases of 2,450% in lines of code and 240% in commits, but only 30% in releases.
Human approval is not sufficient evidence of independent judgment. The cognitive-surrender study described in the talk finds that people agree with incorrect AI answers four out of five times.
Repository navigation consumes real agent work. Guidance can reduce repeated discovery, while long-task capability claims must include the success threshold at which they were measured.

Sonar’s confidence formula treats intent, guide rails, independent verification and auditable evidence as jointly necessary. Better generation does not eliminate the need to verify the result or demonstrate that it passed.

Read customer metrics by their actual denominator: being more likely to report a very positive impact is different from measuring an equivalent percentage improvement in security, delivery speed or outages.

He describes tools and specialized roles as a reinforcing loop, where better retrieval enables new workflows and more knowledge production. title: What Is an Inference Engine, Anyway? — Charles Frye, Modal
reason: Inference-engine architecture dominates; deployment-specific correctness/observability checks are a short section, not a developed benchmark or quality-evaluation protocol.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Charles Frye examines how inference engines organize the work behind model-serving APIs, using SGLang and vLLM as reference points. He distinguishes interactive chatbots, background agents, and data processors by latency budgets, prompt and output lengths, throughput demands, and prefix reuse. Prefill processes input tokens, while decode repeatedly generates output tokens; their different arithmetic profiles shape scheduling and deployment choices. Requests pass through server IO, tokenization, resource scheduling, batched model execution, and detokenization. Frye emphasizes that the scheduler can constrain GPU utilization despite performing much less computation, and explains why separate processes and Python's accelerator ecosystem are common architectural choices. Model execution draws heavily on shared attention, matrix-multiplication, and expert-routing kernel libraries, while engines differentiate through batching and resource management. KV caching and shared-prefix reuse save computation but require careful capacity and layout management; cache thrashing signals deployment pressure. CUDA graphs reduce repeated CPU kernel-launch work. Speculative decoding proposes several tokens for parallel target-model verification, preserving the target distribution with appropriate sampling, subject to numerical effects. Frye recommends evaluating the actual deployment, logging token IDs to investigate tokenizer and chat-template bugs, and retaining metrics and traces for regressions and replica differences. In a museum placard generator example, increased traffic raises time to first token and intertoken latency; additional replicas relieve the queue. He closes with profiling tools and compact reference engines for studying implementation details.
summary_key_points: Describe workloads using input and output lengths, request rate, prefix reuse and latency budgets. Prefill and decode place different demands on the same engine.
The scheduler can bottleneck the GPU despite doing much less computation. It must prepare useful batches quickly enough to keep execution moving.
KV caching saves repeated computation, CUDA graphs save repeated host launch work, and speculative decoding lets the target check several proposed tokens together.
Evaluate the deployed engine for correctness, log token IDs for tokenizer problems, and compare traces and metrics across time and replicas.
In the placard-generator example, a traffic spike increased both first-token waits and intertoken latency. Additional replicas absorbed load and brought the queue back down.

title: Your Code Has Bugs. Lean4 Has Proofs: Formal Verification for Engineers — Varun Pant, AWS

evidence_basis.summary_text: Varun Pant presents formal verification as a way to check AI-generated code against explicit specifications. Lean expresses code and proofs in the same language. Tactics construct proofs through interactive search and backtracking, while a small trusted kernel checks the resulting proof.

title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
reason: Primary content: Kim Maida, who introduces herself as Keycard's founding GTM engineer and head of DevRel, contrasts two staged on-call triage demos. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Kim Maida, who introduces herself as Keycard's founding GTM engineer and head of DevRel, contrasts two staged on-call triage demos. With standing API keys and administrator database credentials, the first agent shares customer PII, drops a billing database without verifying restoration, restarts production and scales a service from four pods to 40 at $420 per hour. Maida connects these risks to Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content and external communication. She argues for controlling access while retaining useful capabilities, rather than relying on approval prompts alone. Her proposed architecture uses OAuth token exchange and a security token service to evaluate requested access, user identity, agent identity and delegation, issuing short-lived credentials scoped to tool calls and downstream resources. She separately describes Keycard's intent-based authorization proposal, where missions constrain goals, actions and limits; she explicitly says it is not a finalized standard. The second demo uses task-based policy governance, not IBA: customer-data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal succeeds, an approved restart remains blocked because the user lacks authority, and approved scaling succeeds because the user's role permits it. The demonstrated controls govern authorization; they do not establish that every authorized agent decision is correct. Per-tool issuance, mission checks and brief credential lifetimes are implementation choices, not universal guarantees of RFC 8693.
summary_key_points: Private data, untrusted content and external tools make agents useful while creating opportunities for harmful data movement and actions. Broad standing credentials turn those opportunities into executable authority.

Delegated token exchange lets a security token service evaluate the user, agent, requested resource and action before issuing short-lived access, with another exchange when an MCP tool needs downstream credentials.
Keycard’s proposed intent-based authorization adds a mission with a goal, allowed actions and limits. The second demo instead uses task-based policy governance.
Human approval remains subject to authorization: the restart stays blocked because the user lacks the role, while approved scaling proceeds because the user has authority.

title: The Half Life of Agent Infrastructure — Ben Kus, Box
reason: Infrastructure adaptability talk recommends customer-relevant evals before migrations, but gives no substantive evaluation methodology.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Ben Kus argues that agent infrastructure changes quickly enough to undermine the usual advice to choose a stack and switch rarely. Drawing on Box's experience rebuilding agents, he recommends preparing teams for repeated change, making underlying technologies replaceable, using evaluations to justify migrations and assessing vendors' ability to adapt.

title: SOTA Generative Media Panel — Dumitru Erhan, Shane Gu & Nicole Brichtova, Google DeepMind

evidence_basis.summary_text: The panel discusses generative image, video and audio models, emphasizing practical editing workflows, the limits of language as a representation, and the difficulty of evaluation. Panelists distinguish visually appealing outputs from realistic or useful ones, describe how human preferences can encourage unwanted aesthetics, and argue that expert feedback and real customer workflows expose failures missed by general evaluations.
summary_key_points: Practical applications discussed include generating video from storyboards and audio references, natural-language video editing, marketing assets, personalized educational materials, and translation.

The panel considers unified multimodal models a possible longer-term direction, while emphasizing that engineering trade-offs and specialized applications still justify multiple models. Transfer between different modalities remains a research question.

Language provides useful structure and access to pretrained knowledge, but the panel argues it cannot fully represent sensory information. Video models and direct media references can complement text, especially for sound, style and other difficult-to-describe qualities.

Joint audio-video generation is motivated by a shared underlying event: speech and lip movement must stay synchronized. The discussion also identifies room acoustics and distance-dependent sound as important aspects of convincing generated scenes.

Default aesthetics require deliberate choices, while instruction following and references should let users steer away from them. A model's tendency to add wedding rings illustrates an overlooked behavior that panelists discuss as possible reward hacking.

Evaluation combines extensive human assessments, live experiments, automated checks and expert workflow feedback. Small group side-by-side reviews help decide between close models, but panelists explicitly clarify that broader human evaluations cover thousands of items.

The panel seeks high-quality media and real creative task trajectories, including intermediate decisions and iterations. Forward deployed engineers are discussed as a channel for bringing customer failures and feedback into model development.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Ben Dicken, introduced in the recording as being from PlanetScale, argues that AI-driven development and traffic growth require infrastructure that supports rapid shipping while containing failures. He explains isolation between the database data plane and frequently changed supporting services, plus primary-and-replica redundancy across data centers or availability zones. For scalability, he describes distributing data and queries through sharding, rejecting excess work through backpressure, and decoupling transactional, analytics, queue, and cache workloads so they can scale independently. summary_key_points: Isolation contains a component’s failure; redundancy provides a replacement when a server fails. Growing fleets need both because individual failures become routine.
Sharding distributes capacity, backpressure limits overload, and decoupling lets workloads scale independently. Each solves a different problem.
A VSchema gives an agent a text configuration to help design while Vitess and VTGate operate the query-routing machinery.
Traffic Control assigns resource budgets to tagged traffic, with warnings or query termination providing explicit responses to overload.

title: Is the Agent Harness Dead? — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
reason: Harness obsolescence and architecture; benchmark comparisons are cited as motivation without substantive evaluation methodology.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Jediah Katz argues that smarter models have absorbed many coding behaviors once supplied by agent harnesses, such as exploring repositories, persisting on tasks, applying edits, and checking work. He describes studies that reportedly found little significant difference in benchmark scores among harnesses for newer models; the studies are presented through the talk rather than independently verified here. Katz calls the mechanism a “data flywheel”: harnesses make harder tasks feasible, resulting usage generates data from which models learn, and obsolete scaffolding can then be removed. He nevertheless argues that harnesses remain essential because they open new task frontiers and provide capabilities models cannot absorb. Grokbot is presented as an example, using long-lived coordinator bots and worker agents for broader knowledge work; its harness supplies prompting and guardrails for communication, risky actions, website workflows, and memory. A software-factory example extends orchestration across bug triage, cloud-based fixes, verification, deployment, and production monitoring. Katz identifies durable harness responsibilities in cloud runtime infrastructure, scoped permissions and guardrails, and efficiency. He expects harnesses to become more modular, rely on composable agent primitives such as event subscriptions, track temporary behavioral shims for removal, and use agents rather than individual LLM calls as their primary building blocks. He closes by predicting that within six months, 90% of agent work will run off the laptop. The supplied sources do not establish the event, presentation date, or a reconciled current organizational affiliation for Katz.

title: From 15% to 90% GPU Utilization: Fix the Data Pipeline, Not the Model
reason: Primary content: The recording metadata identifies Tarun Sunkaraneni of Amazon AGI as the presenter of a multimodal supervised fine-tuning pipeline case study. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: The recording metadata identifies Tarun Sunkaraneni of Amazon AGI as the presenter of a multimodal supervised fine-tuning pipeline case study. Using a Qwen3-VL base model, S3-hosted images and Megatron data-parallel training, the talk focuses on keeping GPUs supplied with data. The serial baseline takes more than 100 seconds to fetch a batch against 15–20 seconds of training, yielding about 15% GPU utilization. The pipeline adds asyncio for image fetching and Ray actors for processing, then a background prefetch queue to prepare batches before the trainer requests them. Prefetching reduces visible loading and transformation waits but complicates checkpointing and resumption and introduces queue warm-up. Ray object references then reduce repeated serialization and copying of large image arrays through the coordinator, lowering communication costs and memory pressure. At this intermediate stage, the reported wait ratio falls from 85% to 20%. Scaling data-parallel ranks and batch size fourfold, with about 200 data streams, exposes a network-card bottleneck on colocated workers. Spreading workers across nodes and enabling zero-copy retrieval together produce a reported additional 50% throughput at scale, despite offering no benefit in the small experiment. The talk separately reports an overall improvement from 15% to 90% GPU utilization. Its central recommendation is to profile each stage and reassess framework settings as scale changes.
summary_key_points: A batch that needs more than 100 seconds of fetching and only 15–20 seconds of training is primarily a data-pipeline optimization problem.
Use concurrency that fits the work: asynchronous requests for I/O, threads where operations release the GIL, and processes for separate CPU execution.
Prefetching hides preparation behind training when the producer stays ahead, while adding queue startup and checkpoint-resumption complexity.
Passing object references lets training ranks retrieve large tensors directly, avoiding repeated copies through the coordinator.
Evaluate configuration at the intended scale: spread scheduling and zero-copy retrieval gave no small-scale benefit here, but together added 50% throughput at large scale.

title: From coding to Knowledge work agents — Karan Vaidya, Composio
reason: Knowledge-work infrastructure primitives and conceptual verification; not substantive eval method or benchmark discussion.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Karan Vaidya argues that coding agents benefit from surrounding infrastructure that knowledge work agents lack. He outlines six needs—centralization, history, context, verification, governance and reversibility—and describes approaches involving shared app access, action records, learned workflow patterns, sandbox review and externally enforced controls. His hiring-outreach example illustrates why successful execution alone does not establish that an action should occur.
summary_key_points: Vaidya attributes coding agents' progress partly to repositories, commit history, tests, review and rollback, and proposes six corresponding primitives for knowledge work.
Centralization brings scattered business information, connections and logins into one place so agents can access the context needed to begin work.

Cross-app action records can give agents usable history and let people inspect outcomes. Patterns in those records can become skills reflecting tool behavior, organizational workflows and individual preferences.

His hiring agent sent technically valid outreach that he describes as a disaster. He proposes checking drafts against prior emails and rehearsing consequential actions with mocked tools for review before execution.
Governance should live outside the agent's prompt memory. He describes deterministic access limits plus policies controlling permitted behavior, such as deletion thresholds and allowed email domains.

He acknowledges that reversibility is difficult and incomplete for knowledge work. He proposes undo where available and sandbox review before actions that cannot be reversed, concluding that surrounding infrastructure is the main bottleneck.

title: Advanced Workshop: Mastering AI Observability — Doug Guthrie, Braintrust
reason: Observability workshop includes calibrated scorers, online sampling, baseline offline evaluations, failure-backed datasets and reviewable improvement experiments.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Doug Guthrie presents a hands-on Braintrust workshop on turning agent telemetry into measurable improvements. He frames tracing as the foundation, then distinguishes targeted code-based scorers and LLM judges from Topics, which groups patterns in user tasks, sentiment, and issues beyond existing evaluation coverage. He emphasizes human calibration of judges and evaluation assets that evolve with the agent.

The demonstration configures a Python support agent built with the OpenAI Agents SDK, verifies tracing, runs baseline offline evaluations, publishes scorers, and enables online scoring with scope and sampling controls. Guthrie adds a custom support-workflow facet and conversation grouping settings, then imports 968 sample traces containing 5,260 spans. The examples reveal order-record lookup failures; the coding-agent analysis also identifies escalation-tool errors. The default issues facet does not produce enough matching outputs for a topic map, illustrating the value of a domain-specific facet.

Loop queries relevant trace data with SQL, and selected failures return to evaluation datasets as regression examples. A coding agent equipped with the Braintrust CLI and an improvement skill investigates traces alongside repository code, proposes changes to tools and scorers, and checks them through evaluations. Guthrie shows a GitHub Actions workflow that packages changes, explanations, and evaluation evidence into a pull request for human review. Questions address hosting, sampling, project boundaries, scorer composition, and restricted trace access. The final demonstration exposes parameterized remote evaluations to a playground so collaborators can adjust prompts and models while execution remains on the evaluation server.
summary_key_points: Traces supply the intermediate evidence; scorers and topic labels make relevant failures easier to find within a large stream.
Custom facets can reveal domain-specific workflow problems that default issue classification misses, as the support-agent record-lookup example shows.
Production failures belong in evaluation datasets so fixes can be checked against both new edge cases and previously preserved behavior.
A coding assistant needs repository access plus selected trace evidence to propose concrete changes. The CLI and improvement skill connect those two kinds of context.
Automation can package code changes, reasons, regression cases and evaluation evidence into a pull request; a reviewer still decides whether the proposal should ship.
Remote evaluations let collaborators change exposed prompts and models in a playground while agent execution stays on the evaluation server.

title: Why 99% Accurate Browser Agents Still Fail — Derek Meegan, Browserbase
reason: Browser reliability measures verified completion per transaction, retries, compounding failure and ongoing environment/model reevaluation.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Derek Meegan, introduced in the recording as a software engineer at Browserbase, explains how to turn browser-agent demos into reliable unattended transactional workflows. He describes three browser interaction strategies: textual representations combining HTML and accessibility information, screenshot-based computer use, and dynamic code execution. Transactional workflows accumulate cost and failure risk at every step but deliver value only upon completion; his thought experiment gives roughly 36% end-to-end success for 100 independent steps that each succeed 99% of the time. He prioritizes performance, then cost and maintainability, recommends verifying concrete completion artifacts, and measures success per transaction with retries rather than per run. Maintenance includes observing both agent decisions and browser behavior, developer intervention, and reevaluation as sites and models change. In a health-insurance portal example, he consolidates document downloading into a deterministic tool, uses OCR to compare document entities with a system of record, moves reusable authentication outside the model, and supplies skills resembling standard operating procedures. The resulting architecture reserves model decisions for necessary ambiguity while reducing steps and improving verification, performance and maintainability.
summary_key_points: Under independent step success, 99% accuracy compounded across 100 steps yields only about 36.6% end-to-end success. Reducing model-directed steps is a reliability lever.
Define completion through a concrete artifact and measure success per customer transaction, including the attempts permitted by its retry budget.
In the insurance example, separate authentication, a packaged download operation, OCR-based verification, and a workflow skill narrow the model’s responsibility to the remaining ambiguity.
Production costs include browser infrastructure, integrations, observability, developer repairs, and reevaluation as websites and models change.

title: How long can your skills be before your agent forgets what you told it? — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
reason: IFScale replication/extension measures instruction-following capacity while distinguishing keyword compliance from reasoning and real-skill reliability.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Laurie Voss presents a rerun and expansion of IFScale, a benchmark measuring whether models include required exact words in a business report. He reports substantially higher capacity in the newer models tested, alongside different failure modes. He emphasizes that keyword compliance does not establish reliable reasoning or real skills-file performance, and argues for checking outputs with evaluations.
summary_key_points: IFScale measures compliance by counting required exact words included in a generated business report; these keyword requirements serve as proxies for instructions.

Voss reports reproducing the older models' decline around 200–300 requirements. Newer models scored 100% on the original test, prompting expansion to a 10,000-word vocabulary; he describes boundaries nearer 2,000 requirements and up to 5,000 for the strongest performance.

He describes four observed failure patterns: DeepSeek omitted requirements, Claude refused requests, Gemini exhausted its budget on thinking, and GPT produced a partial report before declining to continue. He filtered potentially sensitive vocabulary to obtain cooperative Claude results.
The benchmark does not prove that long skills files work or measure reasoning over conflicting requirements. Voss also warns that wording and instruction order can affect reliability.

Voss argues that larger instruction capacity shifts attention toward cost, latency and output verification. His concluding recommendation is to evaluate outputs and revisit older assumptions about prompt size.

title: AI Evals for Cross-Functional Teams — Nachiket Paranjape & Swaroop Chitlur Haridas, DoorDash
reason: Cross-functional evaluation ownership, golden datasets, annotation tools and self-service judge calibration.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Nachiket Paranjape and Swaroop Chitlur Haridas describe how DoorDash's GenAI evaluations became a shared responsibility across engineering, product, strategy and operations. Their platform combines stable APIs, operator-built annotation interfaces, golden datasets and self-service judge calibration. They report lower annotation costs and faster iteration, without giving numerical results in the supplied captions.
summary_key_points: Strategy and operations set priorities and quality standards; product translates requirements into rubrics and workflows; operations annotates; engineering provides APIs, telemetry, datasets and judges.
The evaluation loop captures traces, samples manageable subsets, adds domain-expert annotations, reviews and creates golden datasets, calibrates against them, and monitors results before repeating.
Stable platform APIs let strategy and operations teams use coding agents to build annotation interfaces for their own use cases, reducing the platform team's need to build each interface.
Product managers and operators can run judge calibration through a self-service UI. Showing original and calibrated prompts makes changes reviewable and helps partners assess them.
Judge-prompt ownership varies across teams: strategy and operations, product managers or engineering may own it. The speakers present this flexibility as supporting organizational learning.
The speakers report reduced per-annotation costs and faster iteration from self-service annotation and judge calibration.

title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef
reason: Repeated graph-versus-filesystem tool experiments measure consistency, accuracy, tokens and adoption; checks traces and repository-history leakage.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender present a workshop connecting data engineering context with coding agent reliability. Michael describes Typedef's data context layer: a persistent graph of grain, lineage, metric meaning, and relationships derived from transformation code and checked against real data. His examples show how valid SQL can still multiply rows, obscure a root cause, or silently change a business definition. He advocates deterministic parsing and profiling first, with LLMs used for naming, classification, and ambiguity, and reports an internal task-success improvement of almost 35 percentage points with the context layer.

Callender builds an educational code graph over selected Qdrant Rust crates. tree-sitter extracts syntax, rustdoc JSON resolves canonical symbol identities, and Neo4j stores typed relationships. Two types named PostingList illustrate why text matches alone do not establish identity or dependencies. Graph tools expose blast radius and other relationships to a Pydantic agent; fenic demonstrates inspectable semantic summaries layered over deterministic structure.

The workshop then examines why agents still choose grep. Callender recommends familiar tool names, ripgrep-style output, useful first responses, and explicit measurement of tool adoption. Cached evaluations compare the same model with graph tools versus filesystem tools on 30 questions across repeated runs. Single-shot accuracy is close; the supplied workshop README reports 21/30 versus 19/30, and success on every run of 19/30 versus 11/30. Callender reports roughly threefold lower token use and illustrates adoption increasing from 34% to 72% after prompting changes. These are presenter and repository results, not independent validation. He also recounts discovering incorrect file paths in traces despite favorable aggregate scores.

Closing discussions cover incremental indexing, harder symbol resolution in Python, catalogs as graph inputs, benchmark leakage through Git history, fixed commit-and-diff evaluation snapshots, and small auditable LLM operations. Cross-repository linking and broader business-facing diagnosis are discussed as additional work or product aspirations rather than completed capabilities of the classroom example.
summary_key_points: Valid SQL can preserve syntax while changing grain or metric meaning. Check intended row identity, join cardinality and business predicates before acting.
Derive structure and identities deterministically, check assumptions against real data, and add LLM summaries as inspectable semantic enrichment.
A graph’s capability matters only when the agent uses it. Familiar tool names, familiar result formats and useful first responses help adoption; traces reveal actual usage.
Measure success at least once separately from success on every repeated attempt. Inspect traces even when aggregate results favor the new tool.
Update operational context incrementally, but keep benchmark commits and injected changes fixed so agent comparisons continue to measure the same task.

title: The Agent Behind the Curtain: Building the Oz Cloud Agent Platform — Safia Abdalla, Warp
reason: Primary content: Safia Abdalla explains Warp's approach to building a cloud agent platform that absorbs infrastructure complexity while accommodating developers' workflows. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Safia Abdalla explains Warp's approach to building a cloud agent platform that absorbs infrastructure complexity while accommodating developers' workflows. She discusses sandbox hosting, consistent support across harnesses, agent orchestration, and APIs. Repository triage and review illustrate how agents can support structured human workflows. She closes with a workshop metaphor emphasizing observability, continuous improvement, and cost-effective software creation.
summary_key_points: Platforms should absorb complexity before it reaches users, allowing developers to focus on their work.
Warp supports managed hosting and self-hosting so agent workloads can accommodate teams' infrastructure, security concerns, and deployment practices.
Multiple harnesses should share consistent platform behavior for storing and restoring conversation state and handling agent artifacts.
Orchestration supports delegation through prompts and APIs. APIs expose agents, subagents, compute environments, and artifacts for custom workflows.
Non-engineering teammates used Warp's SDK and API to build Slack bots, including tooling that analyzes social mentions and proposes responses for the social media team.
Abdalla describes agents triaging repository issues, researching context, and asking clarifying questions. Contributed pull requests undergo agent review before human reviewers are notified.
She proposes a workshop metaphor that keeps people central to repeatable software production, with observable processes, continuous improvement, and attention to defects and token costs.

title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
reason: Skill distribution/distillation dominates; the 9/25 versus 25/25 success comparison is supporting product evidence with limited evaluation protocol, not sustained evaluation discussion.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Rafal Wilinski, introduced in the recording as a founding engineer at Runlayer, proposes turning agent experience into reusable company knowledge. He defines skills as playbooks loaded through progressive disclosure and argues that they help steer long-running agents away from costly wrong trajectories. He identifies three adoption barriers: developer-centric local workflows, the effort required to write playbooks, and uneven client support. His proposed distribution layer is a governed remote MCP server that searches and serves relevant skills; he says Runlayer uses MCP tools because resource support is mixed. Drawing on Voyager's reusable Minecraft skill library, he describes distilling skills from agent traces, with failed runs exposing missing guardrails and edge cases. He reports that a Chromium-fork-on-AWS-Lambda task using Sonnet 4.6 improved from 36% to 100% success after a distilled skill was reused, without supplying sample size or evaluation protocol. At company scale, similar runs feed a distiller, skills undergo checks including prompt injection and PII screening, and an MCP gateway distributes them. Wilinski argues that this organizational flywheel reduces repeated exploration and preserves hard-won procedures across model changes, creating a company-specific knowledge advantage.
summary_key_points: Skills use progressive disclosure: a short description helps an agent find relevant knowledge, then the full procedure enters its context to guide the attempt.
MCP can distribute skills from a central server that selects procedures by query and role. Runlayer uses tools because MCP resource support is uneven.
Successful traces supply reusable routes; failed traces expose missing guardrails, dependencies and edge cases that can improve the procedure.
In the reported Chromium-on-AWS-Lambda evaluation using Sonnet 4.6, success rose from 9/25 runs (36%) without a skill to 25/25 (100%) with the distilled skill.
Company-wide learning requires more than distillation: candidate skills pass checks, enter a shared library and reach future agents through the MCP gateway.
