title: Skill issue: stop deploying vision language models, use them with Skills — Merve Noyan, Hugging Face
reason: Two VLM judges filter bounding-box labels; examines judge disagreement, human prompt review and ground-truth versus unvalidated vision evaluations.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Merve Noyan advocates using vision language models to label and evaluate training data, then deploying task-specific vision models. She presents an agent-assisted pipeline that trains RF-DETR from unlabeled images, reports road-sign and document-parsing results, and explains limitations involving judge disagreement, prompt review, and inappropriate data augmentation.
summary_key_points: Noyan argues that task-specific vision models are better suited to real-time applications and emphasizes checking model licenses.
The pipeline uses a VLM to label images, two smaller VLM judges to evaluate annotations, and the retained annotations to train RF-DETR. Judges receive images with bounding boxes overlaid.
She reports approximately three to four dollars for an entire pipeline run, using serverless inference and Hugging Face jobs.

Road-sign evaluation uses ground-truth annotations. For document parsing, she shows a trained detector finding a signature missed by the labeling model, but does not report equivalent ground-truth evaluation.

Because one judge rejects substantially more examples, she retains an example when either judge approves it. Human review remains necessary for generated judge prompts, and coding agents need guidance to avoid harmful augmentations such as flipping traffic signs or changing traffic-light colors.

The toolkit also exposes selected segmentation, pose, detection, OCR, and depth models as agent tools. Planned additions include image-guided detection, intersection-over-union comparison of boxes, and segmentation support.

title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
reason: Observational organization-level developer productivity/adoption research, not evaluation of an agent or model on tasks.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Justin Reock, who introduces himself as DX's deputy CTO, presents five trends in AI-assisted software development, drawing on research he says covers about 200,000 engineers. He reports rising deployment frequency alongside greater change-failure-rate volatility, while cautioning that velocity metrics are proxies for value and that release pipelines and testing also affect quality. Perceived maintainability rose almost 4%, but change confidence fell 6%; average pull requests grew from roughly 44 to 72 lines, and sentiment about incremental delivery fell 10%. Juniors use AI more, while staff+ engineers reportedly save similar time with fewer tokens; smaller companies show greater time savings. Reock recommends measuring utilization, impact and cost, comparing usage cohorts against established productivity and quality metrics. He connects AI readiness to documentation, modular code, reliable CI and stable tests, and describes gathering feedback from agents about context and human steering. He reports median PR-throughput gains of 7.7%, a 13% average and top gains around 70%, arguing that wider workflow bottlenecks limit the benefit of faster code generation. His closing examples include Morgan Stanley's legacy-code analysis agent, with a claimed 300,000 annual hours saved; Zapier's administrative automation and claimed 15% greater value per engineer; and Spotify's incident-context agent for SREs. These case-study figures are attributed to the speaker rather than independently verified.
summary_key_points: Deployment frequency and PR throughput describe work moving through the system. Read them alongside failure rates, review burden and business value.
Fast generation beside slow builds can encourage larger PRs. Improving validation helps preserve small, understandable changes.
AI utilization is not the same as efficiency: senior engineers report similar time savings to juniors while spending fewer tokens.
Measure utilization, impact and cost together, and use agent feedback to locate friction in specific use cases.
Look beyond generation for the limiting step. Legacy-code discovery, coordination, review and incident preparation are all concrete targets in the closing examples.

title: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Any Good: Evals With Phoenix & Claude — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
reason: Phoenix evaluation workshop: trace failures, faithfulness/actionability judges, human labels, dev/test splits, repeated experiments and CI acceptance criteria.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Laurie Voss leads a hands-on workshop on evaluating a Claude-powered financial analyst. She traces its research and report-writing turns in Arize Phoenix, then recommends reading traces before defining complementary code, LLM-judge and human evaluations. One Tesla report combines figures from different searches into a 116% analyst consensus, illustrating a reasoning failure visible in the trace.

A built-in correctness judge fails all 16 reports partly because it cannot verify fresh information; Voss instead supplies search results and research notes to a faithfulness judge. She builds an actionability judge, compares it with human labels, and discusses rubric ambiguity, dev/test splits and precision and recall. In her prompt experiment, actionability rises from 5/16 to 48/48 across repeated runs, while faithfulness remains poor at 3/48. A Haiku 5.5 comparison improves faithfulness but produces a strongly conservative pattern. She closes by demonstrating CI acceptance criteria and recommending ongoing sampling of production traffic.
summary_key_points: Read traces before choosing evals: the Tesla consensus combined percentages from different search results into an impossible total.
Give judges the evidence needed for their question. Faithfulness to supplied research is different from independent factual correctness.
Compare judge labels with carefully produced human labels, and inspect disagreements before tightening the rubric.
The prompt experiment improved actionability while faithfulness remained poor; the model comparison improved consistency partly by repeatedly recommending hold.
Reuse established evals in CI and sample real traffic for sustained quality changes after release.

title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
reason: Security workshop tests prompt/tool injection across exposed and protected environments, distinguishes enforcement from detection and uses traces to inspect failure.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee lead a hands-on workshop about excessive agent permissions using BurritoBot, a deliberately permissive food-ordering assistant connected to a Kubernetes platform. Participants persuade it to deploy an external container image and retrieve a fictional secret recipe. A marketing story helps a deployment request succeed, while other requests receive inconsistent model refusals. The presenters use these variations to argue that application boundaries must not depend on a model choosing to refuse.

The workshop compares three configurations: an exposed shared cluster, a second cluster with infrastructure controls, and an environment for toggling AI-specific filters. Kyverno successfully blocks the external-image deployment through admission policy; network egress controls are discussed but not demonstrated. Intended runtime protection fails to prevent recipe access, prompting a discussion of detection, response, and preventive enforcement rather than a claim of successful protection. The agent uses kagent, a guard proxy with LLM Guard, and Amazon Bedrock.

The filtering demonstrations distinguish sensitive output redaction after model processing from input blocking before the main model call. An accidentally enabled input filter interrupts the output demonstration before the presenters turn it off and show redaction. A weather tool illustrates prompt injection through tool descriptions: it couples a legitimate weather request with instructions to read internal configuration, and a later trace shows that configuration tool being called. OpenTelemetry traces viewed in Datadog expose prompts, tools, results, and cost information, while also raising concerns about sensitive data entering telemetry. The closing discussion connects agent security to established CI/CD, identity, network, and artifact controls, and proposes evaluating AI workflows by their boundaries, economic value, and verifiable outputs. Attendee environment provisioning encounters problems during the session; the presenters share the platform repository for further exploration.
summary_key_points: A persuasive business story changed BurritoBot's willingness to deploy an image; Kubernetes admission policy supplied a separate decision about whether deployment was allowed.
Runtime detection followed by a response differs from preventing an operation. The workshop's intended filesystem block failed, even though the distinction remains useful.
Output filtering can redact an answer after generation; input filtering can reject a request before main-model processing. Their costs and protection points differ.
A weather tool description induced internal configuration access by presenting it as a prerequisite. Traces exposed the additional tool call.
Prompts and tool results make traces useful for investigation, but raw customer input can also put unwanted sensitive data into telemetry.
Evaluate an AI workflow by its known boundaries, worthwhile cost and independently verifiable output.

title: One Operator, Many Drones: Inside Skydio's Autonomy Stack — Suchet Bargoti, Skydio
reason: Primary content: Suchet Bargoti demonstrates remote operation of multiple docked drones and explains Skydio's approach to drones as infrastructure. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Suchet Bargoti demonstrates remote operation of multiple docked drones and explains Skydio's approach to drones as infrastructure. He describes fleet orchestration, a flight-data learning cycle, edge and cloud autonomy, shared maps, object tracking, and VLM agents using drone tools. He emphasizes the observability and reliability challenges of fully end-to-end learning in physical systems.
summary_key_points: The opening demonstration includes drones in San Mateo and Colorado, hands-off car tracking, and a fleet return-to-dock command; Bargoti later reports that all landed.
Bargoti argues that assigning a skilled pilot to each drone does not scale with demand, motivating fleet control through higher-level objectives.
Flight logs feed retraining and evaluation, with attention to removing private information and making customer data sharing clear.
Immediate autonomous actions run on the drone, while cloud inference can support heavier computation and longer-term planning. Video quality under limited bandwidth affects this division.
Maps combine prior information with building, road, and power-line data for navigation. Fleet observations feed map updates that can be shared across drones.
Tracking models reason about objects hidden by buildings. A separate VLM example finds a white Jeep and uses drone APIs and tracking tools to follow it.
Fully end-to-end learning remains exploratory because diagnosing failures and guaranteeing the reliability required by physical systems are difficult.

title: How We Got LLMs to Recommend Our Open Source Library — Christopher Burns, Inth
reason: Primary content: Christopher Burns describes changes to c15t’s documentation and packages intended to help agents discover, understand, and install the library. Evaluation, benchmarking or output-verifier methodology is absent or incidental in the available publisher summary.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Christopher Burns describes changes to c15t’s documentation and packages intended to help agents discover, understand, and install the library. He reports that LLM recommendations became its largest inbound source and discusses concise documentation indexes, Markdown delivery, documentation tools, and package-bundled guidance. He presents these as evolving practical observations rather than definitive findings.
summary_key_points: Burns says onboarding responses began spiking on April 13 and identified LLM recommendations as the largest inbound source.
The team combined multiple documentation improvements into a framework-neutral pipeline that generates agent-facing outputs from MDX.
He recommends a manually curated llms.txt and a page index with links and short descriptions, reporting that about 40 useful lines outperformed 1,000 lines of noise in their testing.
He proposes serving Markdown through .md URLs, content negotiation, and a mode=agent query parameter to accommodate different agent capabilities.
He describes early WebMCP support exposing tools to search documentation, retrieve pages, and ask documentation questions.

Burns emphasizes bundling Markdown documentation and an AGENTS.md file inside packages because coding agents inspect repositories and node_modules. He reports almost 50% token savings across multiple models.
He stresses ongoing iteration as agent behavior and readiness tests change. For ordinary websites, he recommends Markdown versions of pages and manually maintained documentation indexes.

title: Turning My Obsidian Vault Into a Local AI Engineer — Filip Makraduli, Superlinked
reason: Local OCR/redaction serving architecture; judge-bias warnings and benchmark claims are brief, not evaluation methodology.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Filip Makraduli demonstrates an Obsidian document workflow that offloads OCR, entity extraction, and redaction from Claude Code to an MCP server backed by Superlinked Inference Engine. Using synthetic inbox documents, he shows an NDA redaction workflow and scanned contracts converted into redacted Markdown. The intended benefits are smaller agent context, reduced token spending, and processing sensitive material on infrastructure the operator controls; the demonstration itself uses a managed cluster. He explains the host–MCP server–GPU worker architecture, tool-only protocol boundary, per-worker batching, heterogeneous worker pools, autoscaling, model hot swapping, and task-specific LoRAs. He reports embedding benchmark results of roughly tenfold lower price and 99.8% of a frontier comparator's quality on MTEB tasks, without enough detail here to independently validate those figures. Deployment resources include Helm charts, Kubernetes, and Terraform. Task-aware routing that considers warm models and councils of models are future directions, not demonstrated capabilities. He also describes thinking tokens consuming a summarization budget and warns about biased judges and evaluation gaming. Audience questions expose an unresolved privacy boundary: an agent with raw-file access could read sensitive content before invoking redaction. The discussion proposes further evaluation, stronger guardrails, separated file access, or a private harness rather than establishing a guaranteed privacy boundary.
summary_key_points: Preprocessing a scan into redacted Markdown changes what the main agent needs to consume: OCR extracts the text, and redaction masks sensitive values before the intended handoff.
MCP separates the agent’s tool interface from SIE’s model-serving infrastructure, where worker pools, per-worker batching, autoscaling and model swapping support different workloads.
The proposed model router would consider both task requirements and GPU state: a warm model can be preferable to a nominally cheaper model that needs reloading. This remains roadmap work.

Model configuration must produce the required artifact. A summarizer that spends its generation on thinking and returns little or no summary is a concrete failure, even if inference runs successfully.
Private processing and redacted tool responses do not alone prevent the agent from reading raw files first. File permissions, harness design and evaluation must address that earlier access path.

title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
reason: Context-engine simulator A/B tests the same task with and without context, alongside cost/latency comparisons and code-review regression diagnosis.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Peter Werry, identified in the recording metadata as a founding engineer at Unblocked, explains how context engines connect institutional knowledge from code, documentation, pull requests and conversations into task-specific, personalized, permissions-aware context. He closes with a local, open-source context engine simulator that constructs task-specific context bundles and A/B tests the same task with and without context.

Schema discovery and identity matching can use procedural methods, reserving the model for query synthesis or ambiguous matches.

title: Training Taste — Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs
reason: Measures AI design homogenization and slop with small classifiers and structured inference-time verification.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Thais Castello Branco describes efforts to measure and reduce repetitive, context-insensitive AI design. She reports research on website homogenization and small classifiers for detecting slop, then outlines approaches that combine deliberate creative variation, structured brand guidance, and verification at inference time.
summary_key_points: She distinguishes design properties that can gain expert agreement under specific context, such as contrast and alignment, from aesthetics, where disagreement calls for a more data-driven approach.
She identifies three characteristics of slop: repetition, lack of fit to context, and low intent. She argues systems should help users clarify their intent.

She reports analyzing over two million websites from roughly ten years and comparing them with generated sites. Her reported finding is that palettes and layouts were becoming more homogeneous before AI, while AI increased repetition across different contexts.

Her team mined website features and trained small classifiers, called probes, to detect individual characteristics. She reports that combining their occurrence frequencies predicted slop better than most LLM-as-judge methods they compared against.

She argues inference-time interaction is essential for understanding user context and intent. Her proposed creativity system deliberately diverges on selected design rules while retaining category expectations, rather than relying on increased model temperature.
She describes a brand API in beta that extracts structured components from a brand URL, giving agents guidance and providing criteria for evaluating whether their output follows the brand.

title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
reason: MCP redesign feeds extraction confidence/evidence into quality improvement, penalizes unsupported assumptions in evals and requires human-verifiable workflows.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Abhi Arya, identified by the recording metadata and introducing himself as working on product at Reducto, frames agent-first software as an architecture and accountability problem: who bears the cost when an agent is wrong? He contrasts unrestricted auto mode, a human interface with a limited chatbot bolted on, and agent capabilities designed in service of users who can verify the work. Reducto's initial MCP server exposed every API endpoint as a tool. Although a curated demo worked, team use produced confidently assembled document workflows that neither users nor the agent could explain. Arya describes deleting that implementation and replacing it with fewer tools encoding real workflow structure, including a classify-to-extract operation and a snapshot tool returning live pipeline state and specific errors. Pair structured operations with live-state snapshots so the agent can reference the actual pipeline, including specific errors, instead of guessing its current configuration.
Handle output uncertainty with extraction feedback and task uncertainty with clarifying questions. Evaluations should penalize unsupported assumptions rather than reward confident completion.
Logged overrides, low confidence and questions can feed longer-term guidance. The proposed learning loop improves the context around future agent work.
Design for the person accountable downstream: they need to understand what the agent built and discover mistakes quickly enough to act.

Cross-model disagreement can focus review, but shared assumptions can produce unanimous errors. Preserve domain-specific checks for categories, dates and sign conventions.
Optimize bounded, checked work segments against known intermediates, and preserve the context and evidence needed to reuse them.

title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Micah Silverman, Snyk
reason: Security workshop includes repeated chatbot red teaming, tool-poisoning inspection and explicit evaluation of confidentiality boundaries; general security remains broader than evals.

evidence_basis.summary_text:
Micah Silverman presents Snyk’s six-module AI Security Engineer Foundations workshop, covering OWASP LLM risks, shadow AI, threat modeling, MCP security, secure agentic development and red teaming. His recurring argument is that prompts cannot substitute for access controls: systems should restrict the data, credentials, tools and environments available to a model, while validating inputs and downstream outputs. A student-assistant design illustrates this through a proposed restricted database view that excludes confidential grades instead of merely instructing the chatbot to hide them.

For shadow AI, Silverman recommends continuous AI bills of materials and approved alternatives to prohibited tools. In a live Evo demonstration, he inventories models, datasets, MCP servers and skills, then creates a policy against Salesforce models that flags an existing BLIP component. He proposes CI checks against inventory baselines; the baseline build gate is described rather than successfully demonstrated. Threat modeling extends familiar frameworks such as STRIDE to prompts, memory, retrieved content and tool-driven actions, with updates as architecture and data pipelines change.

The MCP section separates malicious tool descriptions from vulnerabilities in server code. Silverman pairs agent scans for tool poisoning with dependency and source analysis, using Framelink’s historical shell-command injection vulnerability as an example. His secure development playbook adds isolated environments, constrained credentials, approval gates, sandboxing, verified dependencies and monitoring, including defenses against hallucinated-package slopsquatting. The final Grade Your Chatbot exercise exposes a confidentiality boundary through a refusal mentioning grades, but the demonstrated follow-up prompts do not disclose the grades or recover a flag. Silverman emphasizes repeated testing because model behavior varies.
summary_key_points: Prompt instructions and remembered rules influence behavior; external permissions determine whether sensitive data and destructive operations are available.
Assess every permission path an agent can use, including an authenticated browser that may allow actions blocked by a direct integration.
An AI BOM can support policy findings and proposed CI gates, but it must cover models, datasets, agents and pipelines and remain current.
MCP security needs both inspection of model-facing tool descriptions and source/dependency analysis of the server implementation.
The final chatbot exercise reveals a confidential category but extracts no grades. Failed prompts are bounded testing results, not proof that the system cannot disclose its available data.

title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
reason: Domain experts turn planning judgment into skills tested on five-to-ten real cases, with independent reviewers and accountable ongoing maintenance.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Matthew Ragone, who introduces himself as a financial planner and planning-team AI adoption lead at Range, describes how nontechnical staff build agent skills from their professional judgment. Agents draft cash flow or insurance analyses while planners work with other clients; a planner reviews and adjusts every recommendation before sending it, and agents never send directly to clients. His five-step method is to pick a frequent, relatively simple workflow whose output is easy to judge; teach it using real cases while narrating decisions; package the procedure with required questions and explicit limits; test and revise it over five to ten real-case runs; and ship it with an accountable owner and a reviewer other than the author. Owners maintain skills as processes and tax rules change. Ragone reports that, six months into adoption, Range had 24 skills, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the approach without a mandate. He argues that the central challenge is capturing firm-specific expertise, testing it and maintaining accountability as colleagues begin relying on it.
summary_key_points: An agent can prepare another client’s analysis while a planner is on a call, but a planner reviews every recommendation and controls delivery.
Start with repeated, relatively simple work whose quality the author can judge quickly. Teach it through real cases and explain why each action matters.
A useful skill includes required questions and limits on independent action, alongside the steps for completing the task.
Run five to ten real cases before sharing, correct missing questions and confident mistakes, and assign both a maintenance owner and an independent reviewer.

title: Modality Misalignment and Originality Attribution in Short-Form Video — Aditya Gautam, Meta
reason: Video-agent pipeline evaluates precision/recall/F1, retrieval and tool failures, cost/latency and judge drift against humans, then traces errors before retraining.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Aditya Gautam describes a system for detecting unexpected content changes within short-form videos and identifying copied or transformed content for attribution. The presentation divides perception, retrieval, and review among three agents powered by specialized small vision-language models, then discusses domain-specific training, human review, evaluation, and optimizations for large-scale processing.
summary_key_points: The two problems are unexpected temporal content changes within a video and unoriginal content that complicates source attribution. The data includes adversarial uploads, multilingual text, drift, and unclear ground truth.

The perceiver divides videos around temporal changes rather than a fixed frame rate and produces clip embeddings, tags, OCR, descriptions, and timestamps. The reviewer analyzes those structured signals for anomalies.

The retriever indexes topics, embeddings, and entities into inverted, vector, and graph stores to find similar clips and authors. The reviewer also incorporates live reports, reactions, comments, and comment sentiment.

Specialized small VLMs are trained for the domain using in-house visual data and instruction tuning for structured JSON outputs. A continuous DPO improvement loop samples production results, uses an in-house LLM judge and human review, and traces failures to reasoning, tool calls, or retrieval.

Distillation and quantization balance domain performance against inference cost. Evaluation includes precision, recall, F1, retrieval quality, node latency, reasoning budgets, tool failures, token cost, and judge drift relative to human review.
Processing is reduced by compressing similar frames, caching decisions for highly similar viral content, and pruning candidates using metadata such as creator history and authenticity signals.

title: 5 Voice Agent Failure Modes You'll Hit in Week One — Venky B, Plivo
reason: Voice-agent failure analysis includes validated typed fields and field-level evaluations, transcript quality and latency/capability tradeoffs.

evidence_basis.summary_text: Venky B discusses how voice agents fail when moving from demos to production. He recommends balancing latency, cost and model capability; cleaning unreliable transcripts; collecting data through typed, validated fields with field-level evaluations; and normalizing model output before speech synthesis. Turn detection and interruption handling receive only brief closing coverage.
summary_key_points: Measure latency from the user finishing speech to the agent starting audio. The speaker describes a tradeoff between cost, intelligence and latency, and reports that self-hosted open source models have worked for his team's sub-300-millisecond target.

Treat transcription as brittle, especially for proper nouns, numbers and mixed-language scripts. Recommended mitigations include keyword boosting adapted to the call's current state, LLM post-processing and transliteration.

Define data fields before asking callers for values. Validate constraints, confirm suspected corrections or ask for repetition, and evaluate each field as a unit test. The speaker reports roughly 95–97% collection accuracy without model fine-tuning.

Insert normalization between the LLM and speech synthesis: remove markdown and emojis, configure pronunciation dictionaries, slow down for important entities, and explicitly normalize emails, currencies and dates.
The closing briefly identifies turn detection, barge-in and backchanneling as further concerns, but leaves most details on slides and offers discussion offline.
